extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate students learning mathematical proof (introductory discrete math)
extracted.subtask_description: Solve and write clear elementary proofs (induction, combinatorics, relations, functions) typical of an introductory discrete mathematics / proof-writing textbook, showing required steps and common techniques. Exercises include binomial identities, Fibonacci sums, pigeonhole arguments, properties of relations, and function-injectivity/surjectivity/bijection reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of an induction proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove statements by induction by (1) verifying the base case(s), (2) assuming the statement for n (inductive hypothesis), (3) using that hypothesis to prove the statement for n+1, and (4) concluding that the statement holds for all values by induction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: For sums of Fibonacci numbers and combinatorial identities the text explicitly checks the base case (n=0 or n=1), states the inductive hypothesis, algebraically manipulates using the hypothesis (e.g., add F_{k+1} to both sides, use recurrence), and then writes 'This completes the proof by induction.' Strong induction is used when the inductive step requires assuming the statement for all m < n.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use strong induction when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: When the proof of the n+1 case requires the truth of multiple earlier cases (not just the n case), use strong induction: assume the statement holds for all m < n and deduce it for n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Proofs of diagonal binomial-sum identities and some parity arguments employ strong induction; the solution explicitly states 'Strong Induction' and uses values for all smaller m in the inductive step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the Fibonacci recurrence in algebraic manipulations
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving identities involving Fibonacci numbers, use F_{k+2} = F_{k+1} + F_k (and related recurrences) to transform sums and combine terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: To prove sum identities F1+...+Fk = F_{k+2}-1, the inductive step replaces the sum up to k with F_{k+2}-1 then adds F_{k+1} and applies the recurrence to obtain F_{k+3}-1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Pascal's formula for binomial coefficient identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Pascal's identity C(a,b) = C(a-1,b-1) + C(a-1,b) to manipulate and collapse sums of binomial coefficients or to shift indices when proving combinatorial identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Proofs of sum identities like sum_{k=0}^n C(k,r) = C(n+1,r+1) repeatedly apply Pascal's formula and use induction on n; the text also notes treating binomial coefficients as zero when indices are out of range (i.e., identity holds only when 0≤b≤a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat binomial coefficients as zero outside valid range
rubrics_metrics.description: When manipulating binomial coefficient sums, treat C(a,b)=0 whenever the inequality 0 ≤ b ≤ a is false; this simplifies expressions and justifies certain equalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text remarks that C(n,k)=0 whenever it is untrue that 0 ≤ k ≤ n and uses this convention in proofs involving index shifts and boundary terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting regions with induction (lines in the plane)
rubrics_metrics.description: To count how many regions n nonparallel, nonconcurrent lines divide the plane into, use induction: remove one line, apply hypothesis to remaining n lines, then count how many new regions the removed line creates when re-inserted (equal to number of intersections +1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Removing one line leaves n lines dividing plane into n^2+n+2 regions; adding the removed line back crosses the n lines in n points producing n+1 new regions, giving the (n+1)-case count.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove parity properties of binomial coefficients via induction and Pascal
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove statements about evenness/oddness of C(n,k) (e.g., for even n and odd k, C(n,k) is even), use induction on n and repeatedly apply Pascal's identity to express C(n,k) as a sum of earlier coefficients whose parity is known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The solution decomposes C(n,k) using Pascal three times and applies the inductive hypothesis to the outer terms while observing the middle term's parity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish combinatorial identities by algebraic factorization and Pascal
rubrics_metrics.description: For identities mixing binomial coefficients with other parameters (e.g., involving m,n,p), split sums, apply Pascal, apply the inductive hypothesis, and factor to recombine terms into desired closed form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include identities of the form sum_{k=0}^n C(m+k,m) = C(m+n+1,m+1); the text demonstrates splitting off the final term, applying inductive hypothesis, and using Pascal twice with factorings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check relation properties by definition: reflexive, symmetric, transitive
rubrics_metrics.description: When asked whether a relation has these properties, verify each definition explicitly: reflexive (xRx for all x), symmetric (xRy ⇒ yRx), transitive (xRy ∧ yRz ⇒ xRz). Provide counterexamples when a property fails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple exercises apply direct proofs for each property (e.g., parity relation, congruence modulo n, specially defined relations like |3x−5y), and when false give explicit counterexample ordered pairs demonstrating failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove a relation is an equivalence relation by checking the three properties
rubrics_metrics.description: To show R is an equivalence relation, prove reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity using direct proofs (often manipulating integer arithmetic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: relations like xRy iff 3x−5y is even or 4|(x+3y) are shown to be equivalence relations with explicit algebraic reasoning; then equivalence classes are computed by plugging representatives and simplifying congruences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe equivalence classes and partitions explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: After establishing an equivalence relation, compute and list equivalence classes (e.g., congruence modulo 4 yields classes [0],[1],[2],[3]) and note the corresponding partition of the underlying set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples in the text compute [0],[1],[2],[3] for mod 4 and show partitions correspond to equivalence relation classes; also show that equivalence relations on finite sets correspond to partitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide counterexamples to disprove universal implications
rubrics_metrics.description: If asked to prove statements like 'symmetric and transitive implies reflexive', give a concrete counterexample relation on a finite set that satisfies the hypotheses but not reflexivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text exhibits R = {(a,a),(a,b),(b,a),(b,b)} on {a,b,c} as symmetric and transitive but not reflexive, demonstrating the falsehood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting relations and functions using multiplication principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Count total possible relations or functions by treating independent choices per ordered pair or per domain element and raising the number of choices to the appropriate power (e.g., 2^{n^2} relations on an n-element set; |codomain|^{|domain|} functions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: number of functions f:{A}->B with |A|=7,|B|=7 is 7^7; injective/surjective counts use permutations and factorials when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test injectivity by assuming f(a)=f(b) ⇒ a=b and surjectivity by solving for preimage
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove injectivity, start with f(x)=f(y) and algebraically deduce x=y. To prove surjectivity, take an arbitrary b in codomain and explicitly construct (or solve for) an a in domain with f(a)=b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: rational function f(x)=(5x+1)/(x−2) shown injective by algebraic cross-multiplication; surjectivity shown by solving for x in terms of given b (careful with excluded values).

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct explicit inverse for bijections
rubrics_metrics.description: When a function is bijective, find its inverse by solving u=f(x) for x in terms of u and then expressing f^{-1}(u). Verify domain/codomain restrictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: inverses computed by algebraic rearrangement (e.g., f(x)=6−x gives f^{-1}(x)=6−x; more involved examples include rational and multivariable inverses where variables are swapped).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute compositions by substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: To compute g∘f and f∘g, substitute the formula for the inner function into the outer and simplify, writing explicit coordinate formulas for multi-variable cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: given f(x)=3x+1 and g(x)=x^3, compute g∘f(x)=(3x+1)^3, f∘g(x)=3x^3+1; for multivariable pairs substitute coordinatewise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use element-wise (epsilon) proofs for image/preimage set identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove equalities/inclusions of images and preimages (e.g., X ⊆ f^{-1}(f(X)), f(W∩X) ⊆ f(W)∩f(X), f(W∪X)=f(W)∪f(X), f^{-1}(Y∪Z)=f^{-1}(Y)∪f^{-1}(Z)) by picking an element and showing membership in the other set via definitions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text consistently uses element chasing: assume b ∈ f(W∩X), produce an a ∈ W∩X with b=f(a) and conclude b ∈ f(W)∩f(X), etc. For preimages, show x ∈ f^{-1}(Y) iff f(x) ∈ Y and manipulate accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the pigeonhole principle by defining an appropriate map to pigeonholes
rubrics_metrics.description: To apply pigeonhole, define a function f mapping elements to a finite set of 'holes' chosen so that equal images correspond to the desired relation (e.g., same remainder classes or complementary remainders). Then use |domain|>|codomain| to guarantee two elements share an image and deduce the stated divisibility/sum property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: prove among six integers two have same remainder mod 5 by mapping to {0,1,2,3,4}; prove among seven integers two have sum or difference divisible by 10 by mapping remainders into sets like {1,9},{2,8},..., showing collisions imply required property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reason about zero divisors in modular arithmetic using multiplication tables
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether a product [a]·[b]=[0] implies [a]=[0] or [b]=[0] in Z_n, consult or reason from the multiplication table structure (e.g., in Z_5 the only zeros occur when a or b is 0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text observes that in Z_5 the zero entries appear only in the first row/column and concludes if product is zero then one factor must be zero; more generally examine unit structure of Z_n.
